title: More From Every Channel
summary: Wi-Fi 7 keeps most of a wide channel working when part of it is busy, and carries fuller loads close to the access point.

opener.promise: Puncturing, Multi-RU and 4K-QAM: more from each channel
opener.problem: Without puncturing, a small patch of interference forces the whole channel to shrink.

wifi7Adds: Preamble puncturing existed in Wi-Fi 6 for multi-user transmissions only {{puncturing-ax}}; Wi-Fi 7 extends it to single-user transmissions {{puncturing-be}} and adds 4096-QAM {{eht-4096qam-bits}} and multiple resource units per device {{multi-ru-be}}.

beats.heading: One busy lane closes most of the road

caption.headline: One busy lane closes most of the road
caption.takeaway: Without puncturing, interference in one slice forces the whole channel to shrink.

beats.body:
Picture one wide Wi-Fi channel as a road with many lanes leading from the [[access-point|access point]]. In an imaging suite, a neighbouring network is busy in just one of those lanes.

Without puncturing, as on Wi-Fi 5 and for Wi-Fi 6 single-user transmissions {{puncturing-ax}}, the access point has to avoid it by dropping to a much narrower channel: traffic squeezes into the few lanes before the busy one, and the rest of the road sits empty.
beats.bottomLine: Interference in a small part of the spectrum can cut wireless capacity in a room far more than its size suggests.
beats.sceneDescription: A wide road of eight lanes leaves an access point. One lane is blocked by red barriers for a neighbouring network. On older Wi-Fi, the lanes from the blocked one onwards are greyed out and closed, and traffic squeezes slowly into the two lanes that remain.

callout.title: Why one busy slice hurts
points: A wide channel is built from many narrower slices
Neighbouring networks and equipment often occupy just one of them
Without puncturing, Wi-Fi falls back to a much narrower channel
Most of the capacity in the room goes unused

hotspots.technical: A wide channel is built from narrower subchannels; without puncturing, the access point gives up the whole stretch around a busy one.

beats.heading: Close only the busy lane

caption.headline: Wi-Fi 7 closes only the busy lane
caption.takeaway: [[preamble-puncturing|Puncturing]] skips the busy slice; one device can use lanes on both sides{{multi-ru-be}}.

beats.body:
Wi-Fi 7 can keep the wide channel and skip the busy slice. This is called [[preamble-puncturing|preamble puncturing]], and Wi-Fi 7 can use it for single-user as well as multi-user transmissions {{puncturing-be}}, within a set of allowed patterns {{puncturing-patterns}}.

It also lets one device use several separate pieces of the channel at once, so its traffic flows in the lanes on both sides of the busy one. This is [[multi-ru|Multi-RU]] {{multi-ru-be}}.
beats.bottomLine: More of the channel keeps working when part of it is busy, so a noisy neighbour can cost one slice instead of most of the road.
beats.deepDive: In 802.11ax, preamble puncturing applies only to multi-user transmissions, and each station receives a single [[resource-unit|resource unit]] {{puncturing-ax}} {{multi-ru-be}}. 802.11be signals the punctured 20 MHz subchannels in the preamble for single-user and multi-user transmissions {{puncturing-be}}; single-user puncturing uses a defined set of patterns, and the primary 20 MHz channel is never punctured {{puncturing-patterns}}. It also defines multiple resource units: defined combinations of RUs, even non-adjacent ones, assigned to one station {{multi-ru-be}}.
beats.sceneDescription: The same road in the Wi-Fi 7 colour. Only the blocked lane stays closed; traffic flows in all the other lanes, and one device’s convoy, highlighted, travels in the lanes on both sides of the blocked one at once.

callout.title: What Wi-Fi 7 changes
points: Only the busy slice is skipped, within allowed patterns{{puncturing-patterns}}
One device can use pieces on both sides of the busy slice{{multi-ru-be}}
Wi-Fi 6 could only do this when sharing a transmission{{puncturing-ax}}

questions.q: How is this different from OFDMA in Wi-Fi 6?
questions.a: Wi-Fi 6 OFDMA gives each device one resource unit per transmission{{multi-ru-be}}. Wi-Fi 7 can give a device several, including non-adjacent ones, and can puncture single-user transmissions too{{puncturing-be}}.

questions.q: Can any slice of the channel be punctured?
questions.a: No. Single-user puncturing uses a defined set of patterns, and the primary 20 MHz channel cannot be punctured{{puncturing-patterns}}, so channel planning still decides how well it works.

beats.heading: Fuller loads close to the access point

caption.headline: Fuller loads close to the access point
caption.takeaway: Near its [[access-point|access point]], 4K-QAM can carry up to a fifth more at peak{{qam-4k-gain}}.
caption.technical: 4096-QAM: 12 bits per [[subcarrier|subcarrier]] versus 10{{eht-4096qam-bits}}{{he-1024qam-bits}}; it needs a stricter [[evm|EVM]]{{eht-4kqam-evm}}.

beats.body:
Each Wi-Fi transmission is a trip down the road. With [[qam|4K-QAM]], Wi-Fi 7 can pack more into a trip, up to 20% more at the top data rate {{qam-4k-gain}}, by encoding 12 bits into each slice of the signal instead of 10 {{eht-4096qam-bits}} {{he-1024qam-bits}}.

That needs a very clean, strong signal {{eht-4kqam-evm}}, typically a device close to its access point with little interference, such as a workstation in the same room. It is a best case at the physical layer, not an expected gain for every transfer.
beats.bottomLine: Devices with an excellent signal can finish transfers faster; most devices carry their usual loads.
beats.deepDive: 4096-QAM carries 12 bits per subcarrier (2¹² points) versus 10 for 1024-QAM {{eht-4096qam-bits}} {{he-1024qam-bits}}, and 802.11be sets a stricter [[evm|EVM]] limit for it {{eht-4kqam-evm}}. The gain applies only at the highest modulation, which needs a strong signal and little noise.
beats.sceneDescription: Traffic flows on the Wi-Fi 7 road. The stretch nearest the access point is highlighted; vehicles there stand taller with fuller loads, while those further down the road carry normal loads. A label gives the best-case gain at the top rate {{qam-4k-gain}}.

callout.title: Why loads are fuller nearby
points: 4K-QAM packs 12 bits into each slice of the signal, not 10{{eht-4096qam-bits}}
That needs a very strong, clean signal{{eht-4kqam-evm}}, so few devices qualify
Up to 20% more at the top rate{{qam-4k-gain}}, not for every transfer

questions.q: Will every device get the 4K-QAM speed-up?
questions.a: No. 4096-QAM needs a very clean, strong signal{{eht-4kqam-evm}}, so mainly devices close to their access point benefit, such as a workstation in the same room. Devices further away use lower modulation as before.

beats.heading: Same road, same interference, more traffic

caption.headline: Same road, same interference, more traffic
caption.takeaway: Without puncturing, traffic squeezes into two lanes; Wi-Fi 7 keeps more of the road busy.

beats.body:
Side by side, with the same neighbouring network in the same lane: older Wi-Fi gives up most of the channel, and every device waits in the few lanes left. Wi-Fi 6 could puncture only shared, multi-user transmissions {{puncturing-ax}}.

Wi-Fi 7 keeps every other lane busy {{puncturing-be}}, lets one device use several pieces at once {{multi-ru-be}}, and adds fuller loads close to the access point {{qam-4k-gain}}.
beats.bottomLine: The access point can fit traffic around interference and give busy devices more of the channel, so less capacity is wasted.
beats.deepDive: In 802.11ax, each station in an MU transmission receives a single RU {{multi-ru-be}}. 802.11be defines multiple resource units (MRUs): combinations of RUs assigned to one station, which also make puncturing practical for single-user transmissions {{puncturing-be}}. The top modulation rises from 1024-QAM to 4096-QAM {{qam-4k-gain}}.
beats.sceneDescription: Two roads, one behind the other, each with the same blocked lane. On the front road, older Wi-Fi traffic squeezes into two lanes while the rest is closed. On the back road, Wi-Fi 7 traffic flows in every other lane, standing taller near the access point. The roads are illustrative.

beats.heading: Capacity that survives a busy neighbourhood

caption.headline: Big images, even next to a busy neighbour
caption.takeaway: An imaging workstation by its [[access-point|access point]] can get fuller loads and keep more channel.

beats.body: Hospitals are dense radio environments: neighbouring networks, building systems and wireless clinical equipment all share the air. Puncturing and Multi-RU let wide channels keep working when part of the spectrum is busy, and 4K-QAM speeds up transfers for devices near an access point, such as an imaging workstation in the same room.
beats.bottomLine: Wi-Fi 7 delivers more usable capacity in the real, cluttered radio environment of a hospital, not only in ideal conditions.
beats.sceneDescription: Close to the access point, an imaging workstation sits beside the road. Its traffic flows fast in the open lanes with fuller loads, while the neighbouring network’s barriers stay in their one lane.

callout.title: What it means for the hospital
points: A neighbouring network can cost one slice of a channel, not most of it
Imaging files near an access point finish sooner
No new spectrum needed: the same channels carry more

questions.q: What causes this interference in a hospital?
questions.a: Neighbouring Wi-Fi networks, building systems and wireless clinical equipment share the same air. Puncturing lets an access point skip only the busy part of a wide channel{{puncturing-be}} instead of giving up most of it.
